topics.title: Statement and Proof of Pythagoras Theorem
topics.concept:
What is the Pythagoras Theorem?

The Pythagoras Theorem is a fundamental geometric rule that describes the unique relationship between the three sides of any right-angled triangle. A right-angled triangle is a triangle in which exactly one angle measures 90 degrees. The theorem states that the square of the length of the longest side is exactly equal to the sum of the squares of the lengths of the other two sides.

The sides of a right-angled triangle have specific names:

  • Hypotenuse: The longest side of the triangle, which always sits directly opposite the 90-degree right angle.
  • Base: The horizontal side resting at the bottom of the triangle.
  • Perpendicular: The straight upright side that forms a right angle with the base.

Imagine you are sliding down a straight playground slide. The ladder you climbed up is the perpendicular, the flat ground underneath between the ladder and the end of the slide is the base, and the long sloped ramp you slide down is the hypotenuse.

If we represent the lengths of the perpendicular and base as a and b, and the hypotenuse length as c, the formula is written as:

a² + b² = c²

To prove this theorem, we use geometric similarity. By drawing a line from the right-angled corner straight down perpendicular to the hypotenuse, we split the large triangle into two smaller triangles. Both of these smaller triangles share the exact same structural proportions as the original large triangle, allowing us to use cross-multiplication ratios to verify that the squared areas must perfectly match.

Side NameDiagram Variable LabelAlgebraic Formula Element
BasebSecond squared leg (b²)
HypotenusecLongest isolated squared side (c²)

---------

BasebSecond squared leg (b²)
HypotenusecLongest isolated squared side (c²)

DIAGRAM 1: THE MAIN STRUCTURE OF A RIGHT-ANGLED TRIANGLE

                  |\
                  | \
                  |  \
Perpendicular (a) |   \ Hypotenuse (c) [Longest Side]
                  |    \
                  |_____\
                   Base (b)
                  * Note: The small square in the corner indicates the 90-degree angle.


DIAGRAM 2: THE GEOMETRIC PROOF REARRANGEMENT VIA SIMILARITY

         A
         |\
         | \
         |  \
       b |   \ c
         |    \
         |_____\
         C   a  B
         
  Draw CD perpendicular to AB:
         A
         |\
         | \
       b |  \
         |___\ D
         C  \ |
             \| a
              \
               \
                B
  - Triangle ACD is structurally similar to Triangle ABC, giving b² = AD × c
  - Triangle CBD is structurally similar to Triangle ABC, giving a² = DB × c
  - Adding them: a² + b² = (AD + DB) × c = c × c = c²

points: The **Pythagoras Theorem** only applies to triangles that contain a perfect 90-degree angle.
The **hypotenuse** is always the longest side and sits directly across from the right angle.
The algebraic layout is **a² + b² = c²**, where c explicitly isolates the hypotenuse.
A set of three whole numbers that perfectly satisfies this theorem is called a **Pythagorean triplet** (e.g., 3-4-5 or 5-12-13).
To find an unknown leg length, subtract the square of the known leg from the square of the hypotenuse.

topics.title: Converse of Pythagoras Theorem
topics.concept:
What is the Converse of Pythagoras Theorem?

The Converse of Pythagoras Theorem allows us to test whether an unknown triangle is right-angled or not just by checking its side measurements. It states that if the square of the longest side of any triangle is perfectly equal to the sum of the squares of the other two sides, then the angle opposite to that longest side must be a right angle (90 degrees).

Think of it like a quality control test for builders. If an architect connects three structural timber poles measuring 5 meters, 12 meters, and 13 meters into a triangle, they do not need an angle-measuring protractor tool to check the corner. Since 5² + 12² = 13² (25 + 144 = 169), the geometry ensures that the corner opposite the 13-meter pole is perfectly square.

Let us compare the structural workflows of the standard theorem versus its converse form:

Test ApproachKnown Input CriteriaProven Output Result
**Converse Theorem**You know the numerical lengths of **all three sides**You check the squares to prove a **90-degree angle** exists

sections.content:
What is the Converse of Pythagoras Theorem?

The Converse of Pythagoras Theorem allows us to test whether an unknown triangle is right-angled or not just by checking its side measurements. It states that if the square of the longest side of any triangle is perfectly equal to the sum of the squares of the other two sides, then the angle opposite to that longest side must be a right angle (90 degrees).

Think of it like a quality control test for builders. If an architect connects three structural timber poles measuring 5 meters, 12 meters, and 13 meters into a triangle, they do not need an angle-measuring protractor tool to check the corner. Since 5² + 12² = 13² (25 + 144 = 169), the geometry ensures that the corner opposite the 13-meter pole is perfectly square.

Let us compare the structural workflows of the standard theorem versus its converse form:

Test ApproachKnown Input CriteriaProven Output Result
---------
Standard TheoremYou are told the triangle contains a 90-degree angleYou conclude a² + b² = c² must be true
Converse TheoremYou know the numerical lengths of all three sidesYou check the squares to prove a 90-degree angle exists

DIAGRAM 1: THE CONVERSE CRITERIA CHECKFLOW

                   C
                  /|
                 / |
             b  /  |  a
               /   |
              /____|
             A  c   B
             
  If you calculate and find that: (Leg a)² + (Leg b)² = (Longest Side c)²
  Then the interior angle at corner vertex C is guaranteed to be exactly 90°.


DIAGRAM 2: THE TRIANGLE TYPE DETERMINATION TREE

                           Is a² + b² = c²?
                                 |
               +-----------------+-----------------+
               |                                   |
            [ YES ]                             [ NO ]
               |                                   |
      Triangle is RIGHT-ANGLED             Check variation:
                                           - If a² + b² > c²: OBTUSE-ANGLED
                                           - If a² + b² < c²: ACUTE-ANGLED

points: The **Converse of Pythagoras Theorem** functions as a test to check for right angles.
To apply the test, always isolate the **longest side** as c before squaring.
If **a² + b² = c²**, the right angle sits exactly opposite side c.
If the square of the long side is greater than the sum of the other squares ($c^2 > a^2 + b^2$), the triangle is obtuse.
If the square of the long side is less than the sum of the other squares ($c^2 < a^2 + b^2$), the triangle is acute.

topics.title: Application in Calculating Sides and Diagonals
topics.concept:
What are the Practical Applications of Pythagoras Theorem?

The application of Pythagoras Theorem goes far beyond basic triangles. It is an essential tool used to find unknown paths and straight lines hidden inside other geometric shapes like rectangles, squares, rhombuses, and isosceles triangles.

A prime example is calculating a diagonal. A diagonal is a straight line that cuts across a shape from one corner vertex to the opposite corner vertex. When you draw a diagonal line through a square or rectangle, it splits the shape into two symmetrical right-angled triangles.

Let us explore where these hidden right angles appear:

  • Rectangles and Squares: The corner angles are always exactly 90 degrees. Drawing a diagonal creates a right-angled triangle where the width and length are the legs, and the diagonal line is the hypotenuse.
  • Rhombuses: The two intersecting internal diagonals cross each other at a perfect 90-degree right angle. This splits a rhombus into four small internal right-angled triangles.
  • Isosceles Triangles: Drawing an altitude height line from the top vertex straight down to the base bisects it at a 90-degree angle, creating two matching right triangles.
Geometric Shape ProfileHidden Leg ElementsHypotenuse Element
SquareSide (s) and Side (s)Corner-to-corner Diagonal (D)
Isosceles TriangleAltitude Height (h) and Half-Base (b/2)Equal Outer Sloped Side (s)

sections.content:
What are the Practical Applications of Pythagoras Theorem?

The application of Pythagoras Theorem goes far beyond basic triangles. It is an essential tool used to find unknown paths and straight lines hidden inside other geometric shapes like rectangles, squares, rhombuses, and isosceles triangles.

A prime example is calculating a diagonal. A diagonal is a straight line that cuts across a shape from one corner vertex to the opposite corner vertex. When you draw a diagonal line through a square or rectangle, it splits the shape into two symmetrical right-angled triangles.

Let us explore where these hidden right angles appear:

Rectangles and Squares: The corner angles are always exactly 90 degrees. Drawing a diagonal creates a right-angled triangle where the width and length are the legs, and the diagonal line is the hypotenuse. Rhombuses: The two intersecting internal diagonals cross each other at a perfect 90-degree right angle. This splits a rhombus into four small internal right-angled triangles. * Isosceles Triangles: Drawing an altitude height line from the top vertex straight down to the base bisects it at a 90-degree angle, creating two matching right triangles.

Geometric Shape ProfileHidden Leg ElementsHypotenuse Element
---------
RectangleLength (L) and Width (W)Corner-to-corner Diagonal (D)
SquareSide (s) and Side (s)Corner-to-corner Diagonal (D)
Isosceles TriangleAltitude Height (h) and Half-Base (b/2)Equal Outer Sloped Side (s)

DIAGRAM 1: THE HIDDEN RIGHT TRIANGLE INSIDE A RECTANGLE

        _______________________
       |                     / |
       |                    /  |
       |                   /   |
 Width |                  /    | Diagonal (d)
  (w)  |                 /     |
       |                /      |
       |_______________/_______|
               Length (l)
       
       * Formula connection: (Length)² + (Width)² = (Diagonal)²


DIAGRAM 2: THE DIAGONAL INTERSECTION INTERIOR OF A RHOMBUS

                   /\
                  /  \
                 /    \
                /--*---\   <--- The center intersection point forms four 90° angles!
               /    |   \
              /     |    \
              \___________/

points: Drawing a diagonal through a rectangle or square creates a right-angled triangle.
The formula for the diagonal of any rectangle is **d = √(length² + width²)**.
The formula for the diagonal of any square with side s is always **d = s√2**.
In a **rhombus**, remember that the diagonals bisect each other at a right angle, so you must use half the diagonal lengths when setting up your calculation legs.
Real-world problems involving walls, poles, ladders, or shadows can be modeled as right-angled triangles.

questions.q: In a right-angled triangle ABC with the right angle at corner B, side AB = 6 cm and BC = 8 cm. Find the length of AC.
Which of the following sets of side lengths forms a perfect right-angled triangle?
A rectangle has a length of 24 cm and a diagonal measuring 26 cm. Calculate the width of this rectangle.
What is the mathematical name for the longest side of a right-angled triangle?
questions.explanation: The hypotenuse is defined as the longest side, sitting opposite the right angle.

questions.q: Find the length of the diagonal of a square whose side length is exactly 5 cm.
questions.explanation: The diagonal of a square is always equal to side × √2, which gives 5√2 cm.

questions.q: If a triangle has side measurements of 8 cm, 15 cm, and 17 cm, where is the 90-degree right angle located?
questions.explanation: By the Converse Theorem, the right angle sits opposite the longest side.

questions.q: An isosceles triangle has equal sides of 10 cm each and a base of 12 cm. Find its perpendicular altitude height.
questions.explanation: The altitude splits the base in half (6 cm). Height² = 10² - 6² = 100 - 36 = 64 -> Height = 8 cm.

questions.q: A guy-wire is attached to the top of a 15-meter vertical antenna tower. The wire is anchored to the ground 8 meters from the base of the tower. How long is the wire?
If the hypotenuse of a right triangle is 25 cm and the perpendicular is 20 cm, find its base.
If a triangle has sides such that a² + b² > c², what type of triangle is it?
questions.explanation: When the sum of the squares of the shorter sides exceeds c², the triangle is acute.

questions.q: A man walks 12 meters due North, then turns directly East and walks another 9 meters. Finally, he climbs up a vertical tree a distance of 8 meters. How far is he from his starting point?
questions.explanation: Two-step application: Ground horizontal distance = √(12² + 9²) = 15 m. 3D space distance = √(15² + 8²) = √289 = 17 m.

questions.q: The diagonals of a rhombus measure 16 cm and 30 cm respectively. Calculate the perimeter of this rhombus.
questions.explanation: Rhombus diagonals bisect at 90° into legs of 8 cm and 15 cm. Side = √(8² + 15²) = 17 cm. Perimeter = 4 × 17 = 68 cm.

questions.q: An equilateral triangle has an individual side length represented by s. Find the general formula for its perpendicular altitude height.
questions.explanation: The altitude splits the base into s/2. Height² = s² - (s/2)² = 3s²/4. Taking the square root gives s√3 / 2.

questions.q: A rectangular room has floor dimensions of 4 meters by 3 meters, and a height of 12 meters. What is the length of the longest straight metal rod that can fit completely inside this room?
questions.explanation: Longest space diagonal of a cuboid = √(l² + w² + h²) = √(4² + 3² + 12²) = √(16 + 9 + 144) = √169 = 13 meters.

questions.q: In a right-angled triangle, the difference between the two shorter sides is 2 cm. If the total area of the triangle is 24 square centimeters, find the length of the hypotenuse.
questions.explanation: Area = 0.5 × x × (x-2) = 24 -> x² - 2x - 48 = 0 -> x = 8. Sides are 6 and 8. Hypotenuse = √(6² + 8²) = 10 cm.

questions.q: A circle is perfectly enclosed inside a square. If the diagonal of the square is 10√2 cm, find the radius of the enclosed circle.
questions.explanation: Diagonal = side × √2 -> side = 10 cm. The diameter of the circle matches the square side, so radius = 10 / 2 = 5 cm.
